description: Rolling roster of must-read articles on AI and labor markets. Updated weekly.

articles.title: AI Assistance Reduces Persistence and Hurts Independent Performance
articles.author: Grace Liu, Brian Christian, Tsvetomira Dumbalska, Michiel A. Bakker, Rachit Dubey
articles.takeaway: Three large-scale RCTs (N=1,222) provide the first causal evidence that AI assistance erodes independent performance and persistence after just 10-15 minutes of use. In math (Exp. 1, N=307): AI-assisted participants had a 22pp lower solve rate at test (0.57 vs 0.73, p<0.001, Cohen's d=-0.42) and 82% higher task-skip rate (0.20 vs 0.11, p=0.031) once AI was removed. A pre-registered replication (Exp. 2, N=585) confirmed the performance decline (0.71 vs 0.77, p=0.020); notably, 61% of AI users sought direct answers rather than hints, and that subgroup showed the steepest decline (solve rate 0.65 vs control 0.77, p<0.001) and deteriorated relative to their own pre-experiment baseline (-0.10pp vs +0.01 for controls). Experiment 3 (N=168, reading comprehension) replicated both effects with nearly identical effect sizes (solve rate 0.76 vs 0.89, p=0.007; skip rate 0.08 vs 0.01, p=0.008), ruling out math-specific confounds. Proposed mechanism: AI conditions users to expect instant answers, raising the perceived effort cost of independent work — a self-reinforcing cognitive offloading loop. Policy implication: AI systems optimized for short-term helpfulness may be systematically eroding the persistence and metacognitive calibration that drive long-term learning and workforce adaptability.

articles.title: A Technology-Driven Productivity Regime Shift
articles.author: Gad Levanon
articles.takeaway: Levanon documents a structural acceleration in US labor productivity from 1.3%/yr (2013-2019) to 2.2%/yr (2019-2025), driven almost entirely by three technology-exposed sectors — white-collar services (FIIPB), retail trade, and advanced manufacturing — each posting 3.2-3.9% annualized productivity growth while the rest of the private economy sits at 0.1%. Using BEA real GDP by industry through Q4 2025 (since BLS industry productivity ends in 2024) and BLS CES hours, he finds Information sector hours down 6% from their 2022 peak (GDP +8.4%/yr, hours −1.9%/yr post-2022); Professional & business services GDP +3.0%/yr with hours −0.4%/yr; FIIPB's within-industry contribution to aggregate productivity roughly doubled (0.78→1.50pp/yr); advanced manufacturing's contribution quadrupled from a low base. Part is one-time pandemic-era level shifts (firm exit, digital diffusion, e-commerce share), but the compounding forces — generative AI deployment, organizational redesign, platform expansion, and cloud/AI infrastructure buildout — are still early. Implication: weak job growth no longer signals weak output; the pressure lands first on entry-level white-collar work where high-productivity sectors also show weaker demand for junior labor.

articles.title: Ideas for Shared Economic Prosperity in the AI Transition
articles.author: Becky Chao
articles.takeaway: Policy brief synthesizing the empirical case for AI labor disruption — citing Brynjolfsson's 16% relative employment decline for 22-25 year olds in AI-exposed occupations, Brookings' estimate of 6.1M U.S. clerical/admin workers in high-AI-exposure roles who will struggle to adapt, and Azar et al.'s finding (138M worker-firm matches) that ChatGPT cut wages 4.5% at AI-substitutable firms. Lays out a four-pillar policy agenda: (1) modernize the social contract via UI uptake, decoupled public healthcare, an income floor for displaced workers, and four-day-week experimentation; (2) protect workers through transparency rules on AI surveillance, prohibitions on biometric monitoring, and regulation of algorithmic wage-setting/scheduling on gig and on-demand nursing platforms; (3) shape competitive AI markets via NAIRR/CalCompute-style public investment, non-discrimination rules at the infrastructure layer, and data portability mandates; (4) mitigate AI's role in the affordability crisis by banning AI-enabled price discrimination/collusion (RealPage cost renters 4% on average) and shifting data-center electricity costs (residential prices up 10% vs 3% commercial 2022-2024; +6% household increase forecast through 2027) back to the firms driving demand.

articles.title: The AI Jobs Transition Framework: Mapping AI's Near-Term Impact on Jobs
articles.author: Alex Martin Richmond
articles.takeaway: OpenAI's framework sorts all 921 US occupations (147.9M jobs) into four transition archetypes using AI exposure, human necessity, and demand elasticity. Findings: 18% of jobs face higher short-term automation risk; 24% will reorganize as task mix shifts but still need workers; 12% could grow because of AI; 46% see less immediate change. ChatGPT is used ~3x more in jobs identified as most at risk of automation, yet a large 'capability overhang' persists: for high-risk jobs, theoretical exposure is 90% but realized exposure is only 23.8% (66.2pp gap). Critically, CPS data since 2024Q1 shows unemployment rose MORE in the 'less immediate change' archetype (+0.6pp, to 5.1%) than in high-automation-risk (+0.3pp, to 3.6%), reorganize (+0.3pp), or grow-with-AI (+0.3pp) archetypes — undermining a simple exposure-drives-displacement narrative. Authors emphasize these shares are transition-risk maps, not displacement forecasts.

articles.title: Tracking the Impact of AI on the Labor Market
articles.author: Martha Gimbel, Molly Kendall, Natasha Kulsakdinun
articles.takeaway: April 2026 monthly update adds March 2026 CPS and Anthropic's February usage metrics. Headline: no substantial change from March release. Occupational dissimilarity, industry dissimilarity, and exposure/usage metrics remain flat, within historical ranges, or on pre-existing trends. OpenAI exposure quintile shares stable since ChatGPT launch. Unemployed workers in occupations where 25-35% of tasks are AI-performable, invariant to duration. Anthropic Feb 2026 usage data continues to show automation more prevalent than augmentation. Only notable tick-up: dissimilarity between older and younger college grads rose to the high end of its historical range. Measures of exposure, automation, and augmentation show no sign of being related to changes in employment or unemployment.

articles.title: Use of Gen AI in the Workplace and the Value of Access to Training
articles.author: Ali Hashim, Gizem Kosar, and Wilbert van der Klaauw
articles.publisher: Federal Reserve Bank of New York (Liberty Street Economics)
articles.takeaway: November 2025 SCE supplemental questions document that 39% of employed Americans used AI at work in the past year, but adoption is sharply stratified: 58.7% of college grads vs 22.9% non-college; 15.9% (<$50K) to 66.3% (>$200K) by income; 42.7% full-time vs 24.7% part-time. Among users, 66% say AI boosts their productivity (40% finish tasks faster; 22% complete more). Yet 37% of workers say their employer offers no AI tools and 11% say they are actively prohibited. Training gap is the headline: 38% of workers value AI training but only 15.9% get it from employers. Workers without training would pay an average 11.4% of salary to gain it; workers with training demand 24.2% more pay to give it up (loss aversion + selection). 62% of respondents expect AI to raise unemployment in the next 12 months; only 11.6% expect a decline.

articles.title: What will be scarce? The economics of structural change and the post-commodity future of work
articles.author: Alex Imas
articles.takeaway: Imas argues AI won't erase labor — it will trigger a 'post-commodity' economy where spending and jobs shift toward the relational sector (care, hospitality, craft, education) because mimetic/status preferences give human-made goods high income elasticity. Evidence: Starbucks rolling back store automation; human art commands a 44% exclusivity premium vs only 21% for AI art.

articles.title: The Economy Is Growing, Jobs Aren't. Why That Might Be OK.
articles.author: Wall Street Journal
articles.takeaway: WSJ examines the decoupling of GDP growth from job creation as AI-driven productivity gains increasingly absorb output expansion without hiring. Frames the 'jobless growth' pattern as potentially benign if productivity flows through to wages and new kinds of work rather than concentrating at the top.

articles.title: Inside the AI Index: 12 Takeaways from the 2026 Report
articles.author: Shana Lynch
articles.takeaway: Stanford HAI's annual AI Index finds that AI's workforce disruption has 'moved from prediction to reality, hitting young workers first.' Employment among software developers aged 22-25 has plummeted nearly 20% since 2024 even as older colleagues' headcount grows; the pattern repeats in customer service and other high-AI-exposure roles. Generative AI reached 53% global population adoption within three years — faster than the PC or internet — though the US ranks 24th at 28.3%. Clinical AI note-taking tools saw widespread adoption in 2025, with physicians reporting up to 83% less time on notes and significant reductions in burnout. Model transparency is worsening: the Foundation Model Transparency Index average dropped to 40 (from 58). Grok 4 training emissions reached 72,816 tons CO2-eq; AI data center capacity hit 29.6 GW. US lead over China has nearly evaporated. US AI researcher inflow has dropped 89% since 2017. Global corporate AI investment hit $581.7B (+130% YoY).

articles.title: Industrial Policy for the Intelligence Age: Ideas to Keep People First
articles.author: OpenAI
articles.takeaway: OpenAI's policy blueprint for the transition to superintelligence. Proposes public wealth fund seeded by AI companies, 32-hour/four-day workweek pilots with no pay loss, portable benefits decoupled from employers, adaptive safety nets with automatic triggers, 'Right to AI' as foundational access, and modernized tax base shifting from payroll to capital-based revenues. Warns that productivity gains may not reach workers without deliberate policy: 'Workers using AI might well agree that it's increasing their productivity without believing they're seeing the benefits.' Calls for worker voice in AI deployment decisions, pathways into care economy for displaced workers, and public-private energy infrastructure partnerships. On the resilience side: auditing regimes for frontier models, incident reporting systems, model-containment playbooks, and international coordination frameworks. Frames the challenge as requiring a new Progressive Era / New Deal for the Intelligence Age.

articles.title: Where can AI be used? Insights from a deep ontology of work activities
articles.author: Cai, YeckehZaare, Sun et al.
articles.takeaway: Introduces Think/Do/Interact ontology of 39,603 work activities from O*NET 29.1. 92% of AI applications (TAAFT dataset) map to only 6.8% of activities. AI apps grew 6x from 2022-2024 but activity coverage expanded only 1.2x — adoption is deep, not broad. 75% of AI market value concentrated in software/information tasks. 58% of apps target 'Create information' activities. Physical work largely unaffected. EPOCH framework (Empathy, Presence, Opinion, Creativity, Hope) identifies durable human advantages. Inheritance principle: parent-level AI applicability passes to child activities.

articles.title: Economists Once Dismissed the A.I. Job Threat, but Not Anymore
articles.author: Ben Casselman
articles.takeaway: Narrative shift: economists moving from dismissive to seriously concerned about AI labor impact. BCG estimates >50% of US jobs reshaped in 2-3 years. Kinder (Brookings) says entry-level research hires replaced by Claude. Gimbel (Yale Budget Lab): speed and breadth determine how painful the transition. Rock (UPenn): 'I don't think AI has hit the labor market yet, but I think it's coming.' Imas (UChicago): reasoning models were 'paradigm shift.' Korinek (UVA) leaving academia to join Anthropic. Cites FRI survey, Census BTOS adoption data, Brynjolfsson/Stanford entry-level findings.

articles.title: Forecasting the Economic Effects of AI
articles.author: Ezra Karger, Otto Kuusela, Jason Abaluck, Kevin Bryan, Basil Halperin, Phil Trammell, Philip Tetlock et al.
articles.publisher: Forecasting Research Institute (w/ Fed Chicago, Yale, Stanford, UPenn)
articles.takeaway: Most comprehensive expert survey on AI's economic impact. 69 economists, 52 AI experts, 38 superforecasters, 401 public respondents. Unconditional: GDP 2.5% (vs 2.0% baseline), LFPR 61.0% by 2030. Rapid scenario (14% prob): GDP ~4%, LFPR drops to 55% by 2050 (~10M AI job losses), top 10% holds 80% of wealth, labor share falls to 45%. GenAI assists 10.1% of work hours by 2030 unconditionally, 62% by 2050 in rapid scenario. White-collar sector share stalls at 20-21% under rapid. Expert disagreement driven more by beliefs about economic effects than AI capability pace. 71.8% of economists support job retraining; only 13.7% support job guarantees.

articles.title: How much will AI increase economic growth?
articles.author: Stefan Schubert
articles.takeaway: Commentary synthesizing expert debate around the FRI survey. Rapid AI scenario yields only +1.5pp annual GDP growth above slow scenario (+45% cumulative over 25 years). Economists far more conservative than AI experts on growth impact. Highlights social backlash as key constraint (Narayanan), historical diffusion precedent (Novosad), and possibility of Coasean Singularity disrupting adoption models (Imas). Key puzzle: why don't experts expect higher growth even under rapid progress?

articles.title: How AI may reshape career pathways to better jobs
articles.author: Justin Heck, Mark Muro, Shriya Methkupally, Joseph Siegmund
articles.takeaway: 15.6M non-degree workers (STARs) in top AI exposure quartile, comprising 43% of all highly exposed US workers. Nearly 11M STARs in highly AI-exposed Gateway occupations. ~49% of career pathways from Gateway to higher-wage Destination occupations are highly AI-exposed. 3.5M STARs have both high AI exposure and low adaptive capacity (67% of dual-risk workers). Uses Anthropic observed exposure data. Sun Belt and Northeast metros most affected due to admin/clerical/CS Gateway concentration.

articles.title: Plentiful, High-Paying Jobs in the Age of AI
articles.author: Noah Smith
articles.takeaway: Repost of influential 2024 essay with new framing. Argues compute is a producer-specific constraint on AI that preserves comparative advantage for human labor, even if AI surpasses humans at every task. Opportunity cost of AI scales with its productivity, so cheaper compute doesn't eliminate the case for human workers. Key risks: energy competition (the 'horse' scenario), inequality from capital concentration, and adjustment frictions. References Korinek & Suh (2024) model showing wages drop but don't collapse at full automation.

articles.title: Will Wired Belts Become the New Rust Belts? AI and the Emerging Geography of American Job Risk
articles.author: Bhaskar Chakravorti, Christina Filipovic, Abidemi Adisa
articles.publisher: Digital Planet, The Fletcher School, Tufts University
articles.takeaway: Introduces the American AI Jobs Risk Index. 9.3M US jobs vulnerable under median adoption (range 2.7-19.5M), ~6% industry-wide displacement. Information (18.3%), Finance and Insurance (16.5%), Professional Services (15.6%) face steepest risks. Writers/Authors (57%), Computer Programmers (55%), Web Designers (55%) are most vulnerable occupations. Innovation hubs (San Jose 9.9%, DC 9.1%) face highest geographic risk. $757B in annual income at risk (2-15% of total wage income). 4.9M 'tipping point' workers in 33 occupations swing from <10% to >40% displacement.

articles.title: Anthropic Economic Index report: Learning curves
articles.author: Maxim Massenkoff, Eva Lyubich, Peter McCrory, Ruth Appel, Ryan Heller
articles.takeaway: 49% of jobs have at least a quarter of their tasks performed using Claude. High-tenure users show 10% higher success rates, evidence consistent with learning-by-doing. Coding tasks migrating from Claude.ai to automated API workflows (+14% since Aug 2025). Early adopters with high-skill tasks have more successful interactions, identifying a skill-biased adoption channel that may deepen labor market inequality. Average task value on Claude.ai declined from $49.3 to $47.9/hr as adoption broadened to lower-wage tasks.

articles.title: O-Ring Automation
articles.author: Joshua S. Gans, Avi Goldfarb
articles.takeaway: Formal model showing that when tasks are quality complements (O-ring production), partial automation triggers a 'focus' mechanism that can raise worker income. Task-by-task substitution logic is incomplete because automating one task changes the return to automating others. Automation decisions can require bundled adoption even when quality improves smoothly. Linear exposure indices overstate displacement when tasks are complements. The relevant object is not average task exposure but the structure of bottlenecks.

articles.title: How Will AI-driven Automation Actually Affect Jobs?
articles.author: Alex Imas, Soumitra Shukla
articles.takeaway: Applies Gans & Goldfarb's O-ring model of automation to show that AI exposure measures are routinely misinterpreted as displacement forecasts. In jobs with many complementary tasks (consulting, medicine, academia), partial automation triggers a 'focus effect' that raises worker productivity and wages. Low-dimensional jobs (trucking, warehousing) face the real displacement risk because firms have stronger financial incentive to fully automate when few non-automated tasks remain. Whether exposure leads to better or worse outcomes depends on demand elasticity, job dimensionality, and firm incentives -- not average task exposure alone.

articles.title: The History of Technological Anxiety and the Future of Economic Growth: Is This Time Different?
articles.author: Joel Mokyr, Chris Vickers, Nicolas L. Ziebarth
articles.takeaway: Surveys 250 years of technological anxiety across three recurring themes: displacement fears, work dehumanization, and stagnation pessimism. Finds predictions of widespread technological unemployment were 'by and large, wrong' but cautions against trivializing costs to the displaced. Ricardo reversed his own position on machinery in 1821. The Luddite riots were driven more by wages than anti-machinery sentiment. Annual hours worked halved from 2,950 (1870) to 1,500 (1998). Concludes with Amara's Law: we overestimate technology's short-run effect and underestimate its long-run effect.

articles.title: Evaluating the Impact of AI on the Labor Market: January/February CPS Update
articles.author: Gimbel, Kendall, Kulsakdinun
articles.takeaway: Jan/Feb 2026 CPS data and Anthropic's new 'Observed Exposure' metric do not suggest any substantial AI labor market impact. Occupational dissimilarity, industry dissimilarity, and all exposure/usage metrics remain flat, within historical ranges, or on pre-existing trends. OpenAI exposure quintiles stable. No relationship between automation/augmentation measures and employment or unemployment changes.

articles.title: The Best Guide to the AI Revolution May Be Victorian Fiction
articles.author: Martha Gimbel
articles.takeaway: Industrial Revolution novels illuminate what living through epochal technological change feels like. Handloom weavers -- the white-collar workers of their day -- saw real wages fall by half between 1806 and 1820. Recommends Shirley (Bronte), North and South (Gaskell), and A Christmas Carol (Dickens) as guides to understanding technological disruption, labor unrest, and society's response to those who lost out. AI transition may be faster and bigger, but the human dynamics are strikingly familiar.

articles.title: The Displacement of Cognitive Labor and What Comes After
articles.author: Sahaj Garg
articles.takeaway: Stanford grad turned AI startup CTO argues cognitive labor automation is months away, not decades. Reports 4-week engineering tasks completed in 45 minutes with AI. Physical labor automation follows on 5-10 year timeline as AI-compressed R&D accelerates robotics. The identity crisis for displaced knowledge workers may be worse than the economic loss, paralleling Rust Belt deindustrialization at larger scale. Post-abundance world splits into zero-marginal-cost cognitive goods and still-scarce physical/experiential goods.

articles.title: 81,000 People Told Us How They Use AI
articles.author: Anthropic
articles.takeaway: Anthropic invited Claude users to share how they use AI, what they dream it could make possible, and what they fear it might do. Nearly 81,000 people responded in one week — the largest qualitative study of its kind.

articles.title: Artificial Intelligence, Productivity, and the Workforce: Evidence from Corporate Executives
articles.author: Salomé Baslandze, Brent Meyer, John Robertson, Emil Verner, Erick Zwick
articles.publisher: Federal Reserve Bank of Atlanta / Duke University
articles.takeaway: Survey of ~750 CFOs: <0.4% aggregate job loss expected, productivity paradox (reported gains 3x implied), finance leads at >2% productivity growth. Routine clerical roles declining 0.76pp/yr offset by skilled-technical gains. 85.4% of firms expect to invest in AI in 2026.

articles.title: Same Storm, Different Boats: Generative AI and the Age Gradient in Hiring
articles.author: Magnus Lodefalk, Lydia Löthman, Michael Koch, Erik Engberg
articles.takeaway: Swedish population register data (4.6M job ads, full-population employer-employee records): 22-25yr employment in high-AI occupations fell 5.5% by 2025H1 vs low-exposure occupations within same employers. 50+ workers rose 1.3%. Broad posting decline driven by Riksbank rate hike, not AI. Effect ~2x larger for young women. Replicates US 'canaries' finding (Brynjolfsson et al.) in Nordic register data; contrasts with Finnish null.

articles.title: See which jobs are most threatened by AI, and who may be able to adapt
articles.author: Kevin Schaul, Shira Ovide
articles.takeaway: Interactive mapping of 350+ occupations by AI exposure and adaptability using GovAI/Brookings research. 6.1M clerical/admin workers most vulnerable (86% women). Consensus: no measurable aggregate displacement yet, but white-collar jobs first in line. Economists stress humility — predictions have historically been poor.

articles.title: Dalende werkgelegenheid onder Nederlandse jongeren die concurreren met GenAI
articles.author: J. Groenewegen, N. van Limbergen, N. Vrieselaar
articles.takeaway: Dutch youth employment in GenAI-vulnerable occupations fell 13% from Q4 2022 to Q3 2025, while other occupations rose 3%. Job postings in vulnerable occupations down 25% vs <10% elsewhere. ICT sector grew 6.5% but youth employment fell 11%. Mirrors US findings from Brynjolfsson et al. (2025).

articles.title: Productive Individuals Don't Make Productive Firms
articles.author: George Sivulka
articles.takeaway: Individual AI productivity gains (10x) aren't translating to firm-level value. Historical parallel: electrified textile mills saw no output gains for 30 years until factories were redesigned. Proposes 'Institutional Intelligence' framework with 7 pillars for organizational AI adoption.

articles.title: Why the ATM didn't kill bank teller jobs, but the iPhone did
articles.author: David Oks
articles.takeaway: ATMs didn't reduce bank teller employment due to complementarity, but iPhones/mobile banking caused a 51% collapse (332K to 164K, 2010-2022). Task automation within existing paradigms rarely displaces; paradigm replacement does. AI is still in the 'slotting in' phase.

articles.title: Research on AI and the labor market is still in the first inning
articles.author: Jed Kolko
articles.takeaway: Evidence on AI labor impact is inconclusive; disruption pace matches prior tech transitions. Under 1/5 of firms using AI per Census BTOS.

articles.title: Labor market impacts of AI: A new measure and early evidence
articles.author: Massenkoff, McCrory
articles.takeaway: New 'observed exposure' metric combining LLM capability with real usage. No systematic unemployment rise, but young worker hiring slowing in exposed occupations.

articles.title: Introducing AIR: The AI Resilience Report
articles.author: Jared Chung
articles.takeaway: First canonical aggregator of research on how AI is impacting jobs at the occupational level, with implications and actions for job seekers.

articles.title: What Deindustrialization Did to Men, AI May Do to Women
articles.author: Molly Kinder
articles.takeaway: Millions of women in clerical and customer service roles face AI exposure, echoing the pattern of manufacturing's toll on men during deindustrialization.

articles.title: AI is simultaneously aiding and replacing workers, wage data suggest
articles.author: J. Scott Davis
articles.takeaway: Employment declined 1% since late 2022 in the 10% of sectors most exposed to AI. Wages in AI-exposed sectors rising faster, suggesting augmentation and displacement happening simultaneously.

articles.title: Earnings Season Takeaways: AI-nxiety
articles.author: Goldman Sachs Research
articles.takeaway: No meaningful relationship between productivity and AI adoption economy-wide, but companies that quantified task-level AI productivity saw a median 30% gain.

articles.title: Canaries in the Coal Mine? Six Facts about the Recent Employment Effects of AI
articles.author: Brynjolfsson, Chandar, Chen
articles.takeaway: Overall employment growing robustly, but 22-25 year olds' employment stagnant since late 2022. AI-exposed jobs driving the decline for young workers.

articles.title: Artificial Intelligence: friend or foe for hiring in Europe today?
articles.author: ECB
articles.takeaway: Two-thirds of 3,500 euro-area firms use AI. Companies with frequent AI use are 4% more likely to hire additional staff. Only 15% cite reducing labour costs as a factor.

articles.title: The 2026 Global Intelligence Crisis
articles.author: Frank Flight
articles.takeaway: Little evidence of AI disruption in labor data. Forward-looking labor market components have improved. AI data center construction driving a pick-up in construction hiring.

articles.title: Firm Data on AI
articles.author: Bloom, Barrero, Davis et al.
articles.takeaway: Survey of ~6,000 executives: 90%+ report no employment impact from AI over past 3 years. Firms expect only -0.7% employment reduction over next 3 years (US: -1.2%).

articles.title: How AI is affecting productivity and jobs in Europe
articles.author: Aldasoro, Gambacorta et al.
articles.takeaway: No evidence that AI reduces employment in the short run. AI augments worker output -- enabling faster task completion and better decisions -- without displacing labour.

articles.title: AI, Productivity, and Labor Markets: A Review of the Empirical Evidence
articles.author: ICLE
articles.takeaway: Comprehensive review: 35.9% of US workers used generative AI by December 2025. Adoption accelerating but unevenly distributed across industries and skill levels.

articles.title: Measuring US workers' capacity to adapt to AI-driven job displacement
articles.author: Manning, Aguirre, Muro, Methkupally
articles.takeaway: Of 37.1 million workers in the top quartile of AI exposure, 26.5 million are in occupations with above-median adaptive capacity. Not all exposed workers are equally vulnerable.

articles.title: The Projected Impact of Generative AI on Future Productivity Growth
articles.author: Arnon, Smetters
articles.takeaway: ~10% of US work affected short-term. AI will boost productivity and GDP by 1.5% by 2035. Jobs AI can completely replace saw 0.75% employment fall 2021-2024.

articles.title: The Iceberg Index: Measuring Skills-centered Exposure in the AI Economy
articles.author: MIT / Oak Ridge National Laboratory
articles.takeaway: AI can already replace 11.7% of the US workforce ($1.2T in wages). Tech layoffs represent just 2.2% of total wage exposure -- the visible tip of the iceberg.

articles.title: The Simple Macroeconomics of AI
articles.author: Daron Acemoglu
articles.takeaway: AI will increase TFP by only 0.53-0.66% over 10 years. Much less transformative than the hype suggests, because AI can only automate a fraction of tasks in most occupations.

articles.title: Is AI Already Replacing Jobs? A Large-Scale Survey
articles.author: Bick, Blandin, Deming
articles.takeaway: 37.4% of US workers used AI on the job in the past week. Adoption highest among college-educated (52%) and workers earning $100K+ (58%). Survey of 25,000 workers.

articles.title: AI Won't Just Automate Jobs — It Will Challenge the Meaning of Work
articles.author: Vox Future Perfect
articles.takeaway: Explores how AI automation extends beyond job displacement to challenge deeper questions about work's role in identity, purpose, and social meaning.

articles.title: Can advanced AI lead to negative economic growth?
articles.author: Alex Imas
articles.takeaway: Formal models show AGI-driven demand collapse is theoretically possible if labor share collapses and capital owners are satiated, but conditions are extreme. Benzell et al.'s OLG model shows 'immiserating growth' via capital decumulation when wages fall and savings decline. Imas concludes negative growth is unlikely but demand-side forces will moderate AGI growth expectations. Recommends sovereign wealth funds for broad capital ownership.
